summary: Surco tells a small farmer how many months a year the soil in their yard lies bare, and compares it with cheap changes that keep it covered: dry leaves, a crop rotation or a living cover. Bare soil washes away in the rains and dries out in the dry season, and in Panama few farmers get technical advice. Surco combines NASA satellite data (GPM IMERG rain, NASA POWER climate, MODIS and HLS greenness) with what the farmer sees: a phone photo measures green cover on the ground, because the satellite pixel is bigger than the yard. The app works out the local dry season, shows each zone of the yard month by month, and estimates the water deficit in a normal year and in an El Niño year. It runs in Spanish or English, needs no account, works with no signal, and saves a record the farmer can share with an extension officer.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Surco answers one question for a small farm: how many months a year is the soil left bare, and what is the cheapest change that keeps it covered with the crops the farmer already grows? Live app: https://surco.ciberpty.com

It works in eight short steps:

1. Your plot: location (rounded to about 1 km) and crops, with planting dates.

2. The sky: daily GPM rain for the last 30 days, a 7-day rain forecast, rain in past El Niño years, MODIS greenness through the year, HLS 30 m greenness of the yard, and a map with NASA GIBS layers.

3. Your photos: the phone measures green cover on the ground (Canopeo rule), on the device.

4. Water: whether water pools after a storm, plus an optional can test for infiltration (USDA method).

5. What matters: food, water or less work, to rank options that tie.

6. Your year: months of bare soil today, compared month by month with one cheap change the farmer picks (dry leaves, rotation or living cover).

7. Chat: an assistant explains the farmer's own numbers in plain language.

8. Record: a plan the farmer can share by link with an extension officer, who can leave notes. Exports to PDF and JSON.

HOW IT WORKS

The dry season is worked out for each place (a month is dry when normal rain is below half of the reference evapotranspiration, FAO-56 with NASA POWER), so the same logic works in Panama, Guatemala's Dry Corridor, Kenya or India. Each crop follows its FAO-56 stages from a catalog of 55 crops, with Panamanian sources (MIDA, IDIAP, IMA) for local crops. A month counts as bare when estimated ground cover is under 10 %. The farmer's photo replaces the estimate for the month it was taken. The water deficit of short-cycle beds in the dry months uses FAO-56 crop water use and USDA-SCS effective rain, for a normal year and for El Niño years from the place's own history. Every number comes from deterministic code; the assistant only explains.

BENEFITS

- It turns satellite data into one decision a farmer can act on this season, in their own language.

- It corrects the satellite with the farmer's eye: the photo sees the yard, the pixel does not.

- It works offline and without an account, which matters where signal is weak.

- It connects the farmer with the extension officer through a shared record.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

Test it with 15 to 30 farmers and with Panama's Ministry of Agriculture (MIDA) extension officers, measure whether more soil stays covered through the dry season, and extend the crop catalog to other countries with local partners.

TOOLS

Python, FastAPI, httpx and SQLite for the API; TypeScript, React, Vite, Motion and MapLibre GL for the web app (an installable PWA with a service worker). Code: https://github.com/cpu-16/surco (MIT license). Illustrated step-by-step guide: https://github.com/cpu-16/surco/blob/main/docs/GUIDE.md

LIMITATIONS

Not yet tested with farmers. The satellite pixel is larger than a yard, so cover without a photo is an estimate. Dry leaves are modeled conservatively as low cover. The water deficit covers short-cycle beds only. MODIS MOD16 has no data over pixels flagged as urban. AppEEARS requests can take hours.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI)

AI coding assistants helped write and review parts of the code and text. The team chose the problem, the approach, the field data and every decision, and all calculations are deterministic code. Inside the app, a language model only explains results in plain language; it never produces the numbers. Images made with AI assistance are marked "SI-assisted".
